common_name: Mint Julep Peppermint (Sterile Triploid Cocktail Peppermint)

planting.note: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings after the last frost in moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Mint Julep is a sterile triploid peppermint that never sets viable seed, so it must be propagated vegetatively and is best confined to a pot or root-barriered bed to control its spread.

directions: Set out divisions or rooted cuttings in consistently moist, fertile soil, choosing a spot with morning sun and afternoon shade in hot climates to keep leaves tender and prevent scorch. Mint Julep carries a bold, clean peppermint flavor with a faint spicy warmth that holds up well when muddled or steeped, making it a favorite for the classic Kentucky cocktail as well as iced tea and desserts. Because the plant is a sterile hybrid that rarely if ever flowers or sets seed, all of its vigor goes into leaf and stem production, so pinch tips regularly through the season to keep growth bushy and delay the tendency of mint stems to flop and root wherever they touch soil. Water deeply during dry spells, since mint wilts fast once the soil dries out, and cut the whole planting back hard in midsummer to refresh the foliage.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox — Mentha x piperita

common_name: White Anniversary Oregano (Variegated Shade-Tolerant Culinary Oregano)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; White Anniversary tolerates and even prefers a bit more shade than typical culinary oregano, and its cream-and-green variegation is often crisper out of the hottest afternoon sun.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained garden soil in partial shade to full sun; unlike most Mediterranean oreganos that demand baking sun, White Anniversary holds its dense, creamy-white-edged foliage and low mounding habit even in a partly shaded border or woodland-edge herb bed. The flavor is milder and sweeter than Greek oregano, so use it more generously in salads, dressings, and light sauces where its delicate, edged leaves also serve as an attractive garnish. Shear the plant back by about a third after its small white summer flowers fade to keep the mound tight and to encourage a flush of fresh, well-variegated new growth. It spreads gradually into a tidy groundcover rather than aggressively, so division every two to three years is usually enough to keep it vigorous.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or divisions in spring or fall in well-drained, average soil in partial shade to full sun; as a broad-leaved thyme, Foxley tolerates lighter shade and slightly richer soil than the fussier creeping thymes derived from Thymus serpyllum.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil with average fertility in partial shade to full sun; Foxley's broad, rounded leaves are irregularly edged in cream and take on a soft pink blush in cool weather, giving the low mat visual interest well beyond its short spikes of lilac-pink summer flowers. It has a milder, slightly less camphorous flavor than common English thyme, making it a pleasant everyday cooking thyme as well as a groundcover along a shaded path or between shady stepping stones. Trim lightly after flowering to keep the mat dense and prevent the center from opening up and going woody, and avoid heavy mulch or soggy soil, which this thyme tolerates less well than drought.

common_name: Robert Grimm Sage (Dwarf Mat-Forming Culinary Sage)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or nursery transplants after last frost in lean, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Robert Grimm spreads into a wide, low mat rather than growing upright like standard garden sage.

directions: Plant in lean, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, giving it plenty of room to spread since this selection forms a broad, low mat rather than the upright clump of standard culinary sage. The small, silvery-gray leaves have the same bold, savory sage flavor as full-size garden sage but are easier to harvest in small pinches for fresh use, and spikes of blue flowers appear above the foliage in late spring. Because the plant spreads outward rather than up, it works well as a fragrant, edible groundcover along a path edge or spilling over a low wall. Cut it back by about a third in early spring to remove any winter dieback and keep the mat from opening up in the center.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or nursery transplants after last frost in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Compacta stays under a foot tall, making it well suited to containers and small raised beds where full-size garden sage would sprawl.

directions: Plant in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Compacta packs the same robust, savory flavor of standard garden sage into a tidy, dense little shrub that rarely needs staking or hard pruning to stay in bounds. Its small gray-green leaves and violet-blue early-summer flowers make it as useful in a mixed container or edging planting as it is in the kitchen, and its compact size means a single plant is often enough for a household's fresh sage needs. Harvest leaves lightly throughout the growing season and trim the whole plant back by about a third in spring to remove any winter-damaged growth and keep it dense. It tolerates heat and drought well once established but resents wet feet, so make sure drainage is sharp.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: McConnell's Blue Rosemary (Dwarf Trailing Culinary Rosemary)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants or rooted cuttings in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; McConnell's Blue is a dwarf, spreading rosemary that stays low and wide, making it a good choice for cascading over a wall or filling a large container.

directions: Plant in lean, sharply drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. McConnell's Blue is a low, spreading rosemary that reaches only about a foot tall while spreading two to three feet wide, with broad dark green needles and clear deep blue flowers that appear in flushes from late winter into summer in mild climates. The fully flavored foliage works in the kitchen just as well as any upright culinary rosemary, but the trailing habit makes it especially suited to draping over a raised bed edge, retaining wall, or large container. Like all rosemary it is intolerant of wet feet, so plant in a raised or sloped spot if garden soil is heavy, and where winters dip below the mid-teens Fahrenheit, grow it in a container that can be moved to shelter.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Salvia rosmarinus 'McConnell's Blue'
